sources.title: Claude Fable 5.2 scores 65 on Artificial Analysis, highest so far

stories.headline: Anthropic ships Claude Fable 5.2, tops Artificial Analysis at 65
stories.dek: The new flagship and its restricted twin, Mythos 5.2, cost less than 5.1, but independent testing finds Fable slow and very verbose.
stories.body:
Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 on November 9. Within hours, Artificial Analysis gave Fable 5.2 a score of 65 on its Intelligence Index, a result billed on Hacker News as the highest on the index so far. The median for models in its price tier is 40.

The two are the same underlying model. Fable carries cybersecurity and biology safeguards and is open to all users. Mythos is reserved for organizations admitted to Anthropic's Life Sciences and Cyber Verification Programs. Anthropic says both produce output up to 30 percent faster than the 5.1 versions and cost less: $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. An optional fast mode speeds up generation by up to 2.5 times for $16 and $80.

The company's claims are ambitious. It says a team of 1,000 Fable 5.2 agents formalized the proof of Fermat's Last Theorem in 30 hours, against 11 days for an earlier research version of Claude. One engineer had the model coordinate over 1,000 subagents for eight days to build a prototype operating system that boots on a laptop. Anthropic also says Mythos 5.2 found 10.2 percent more vulnerabilities than Opus 5.5 on its internal CVE Rediscovery evaluation. None of these results have been independently verified.

Artificial Analysis paints a costlier picture of Fable 5.2 at Max effort. It generated 275 million tokens running the index, against a median of 72.8 million. Each task took 46.4 minutes on average, versus a 12.6-minute median, and cost $26.54. Time to first answer token was nearly 216 seconds. The model has a 1 million token context window and accepts text and images.

Anthropic itself does not pitch Fable as an everyday tool. It recommends starting most coding work on Opus 5.5 and moving up to Fable or Mythos for the most ambitious, open-ended jobs. Fable 5.2 can also act as an advisor to smaller models or orchestrate them. On the company's FrontierCode 2.0 test, Fable at High effort roughly matched Opus 5.5 at Max effort for about half the cost per task.
key_points: Fable 5.2 scores 65 on Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, tier median 40
Pricing drops to $8 input and $40 output per million tokens
Averages 46.4 minutes and $26.54 per index task at Max effort
Mythos 5.2 limited to verified cyber and life sciences organizations
stories.why_it_matters: Developers get the top-scoring model at a lower per-token price, but its verbosity and slow tasks mean real bills and wait times can run high. Anthropic still points daily coding to Opus 5.5.

sources.name: BleepingComputer
sources.title: Hackers exploit SSHole OpenSSH flaw to breach Linux systems

sources.name: Ars Technica
sources.title: Vulnerability that lets hackers SSH into Linux devices is under active exploitation

stories.headline: Attackers exploit SSHole OpenSSH flaw to break into Linux systems
stories.dek: Exploitation began the day a fix and proof-of-concept landed, with one group installing a Python backdoor on musl-based systems such as Alpine.
stories.body:
Hackers are actively exploiting SSHole (CVE-2026-123158), an authentication bypass in OpenSSH on certain musl-based Linux systems, BleepingComputer and Ars Technica report. Attackers are using it to run commands, steal credentials and set up persistent access. Admins should update to OpenSSH 10.6p2 now.

The flaw, disclosed by researcher Ozgun Kultekin, lets attackers log in to accounts whose password hash is set to an asterisk (*), a common way to block password logins. According to BleepingComputer, an oversized password makes musl's password-hashing function return * on error, and OpenSSH treats that as a match. Exploitation requires specific authentication settings and does not affect accounts with valid password hashes. It can lead to root where the account has passwordless admin rights. Alpine, popular in cloud and virtual environments, is among the affected distributions.

The timeline was short. OpenSSH maintainers shipped the fix on November 5, and exploit code appeared about four hours later. GreyNoise recorded the first successful in-the-wild exploitation on November 7 at 00:46 UTC, roughly 40 hours after the patch. It logged 16 successful exploitation chains from six IP addresses, though the company says these are not representative of broader activity. Previdian saw 20 attempts from 13 IPs in nine countries, and watchTower tied exploitation to botnets and cryptomining. Finnish firm Defused saw only a small number of actors and called the activity not widespread.

GreyNoise says a group it tracks as GT10 conducted "mature intrusions" into its honeypots in Southeast Asia, per Ars Technica. The attackers ran system and container reconnaissance, queried cloud metadata services, tried to read password hashes and root SSH keys, and edited authorized_keys files. One gained root and installed TAC Agent, a Python command-and-control implant with Chinese-language comments that Ars says appears to be AI-generated. GT10 installs Python3 where it is missing. In the observed case the implant never reached its C2 server. GreyNoise also gained access to a GT10 server that revealed potential other victims.

Besides patching, admins can disable SSH password authentication on affected systems. BleepingComputer advises checking for unexpected successful password logins to accounts with * in /etc/shadow, unauthorized SSH keys, and TAC Agent files or startup services.
key_points: OpenSSH 10.6p2 fixes SSHole, released November 5
Exploit code appeared about four hours after the patch
GreyNoise logged 16 successful exploitation chains from six IPs
Attackers installed TAC Agent, a Python backdoor, after gaining root
stories.why_it_matters: Alpine and other musl-based images are everywhere in containers and cloud VMs, so check OpenSSH versions on any exposed instance today. Disabling SSH password authentication blocks the attack if patching has to wait.

sources.title: Google Gemini routes personal Drive files and emails to human annotators

stories.headline: Report says Gemini sends personal Drive files and emails to reviewers
stories.dek: A GitHub write-up topping Hacker News says Google quietly dropped a 2023 promise that connected Gmail, Docs and Drive content stays away from human review.
stories.body:
Google Gemini routes personal Drive files and emails into human review pipelines, according to a report published on GitHub that has drawn 512 points on Hacker News. The author says Google reversed a 2023 promise that personal Workspace content "is not seen by human reviewers."

The report points to an updated Google Help page and an October 16 edit to the original 2023 blog post. According to the author, Google now warns that reviewers may see "the email or file" and advises users not to connect apps containing confidential information.

The author also claims that consumer Gemini with Connected Apps enabled can pull Workspace data during casual chat, without @Drive or @Gmail tags. In the author's own testing, results varied from no retrieval to full ingestion of an email's text.
key_points: A GitHub report says Google edited its 2023 Gemini blog post on October 16 to allow human review of connected Drive and Gmail content.
According to the report, Google now advises against connecting apps that contain confidential information.
The author says personal data can be retrieved during casual chat without explicit @ tags, with inconsistent results across tests.

stories.headline: Rosen Law Firm files class action against Nvidia over Huang affair
stories.dek: The securities-fraud suit says Nvidia misled investors about its CEO's relationship with an alleged Chinese spy, and more law firms are circling.
stories.body:
Rosen Law Firm has filed the first securities class action against Nvidia after CEO Jensen Huang admitted an affair with Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive US intelligence believes was working for China, Tom's Hardware reports. The suit claims Nvidia and Huang failed to disclose or misled investors about the relationship, lied when asked, raised national security concerns and damaged the company's reputation.

Other firms, including Levi & Korsinsky and Schall, Brown & Schwartz, have opened investigations. They cite share drops of 5.5 to 5.88 percent in pre-market trading, and one firm points to an 8.8 percent intraday fall.

Huang confirmed the affair in an internal message on Sunday, Ars Technica reports. Nvidia's board is opening an independent investigation into whether he was the target of a foreign intelligence effort.
key_points: Rosen Law Firm filed the first class action, alleging Nvidia and Huang misled investors about the affair.
Several other law firms are investigating, citing Nvidia share drops of 5.5 to 8.8 percent.
Nvidia's board has opened an independent probe into whether Huang was targeted by foreign intelligence.

sources.name: BleepingComputer
sources.title: N-able takes cloud platform offline after 30+ "zero-days" published

stories.headline: N-able pulls N-central offline after 30-plus zero-days go public
stories.dek: A researcher posted proof-of-concept exploits without warning N-able, saying earlier bug reports to the company went unpatched and unanswered.
stories.body:
N-able has taken its hosted N-central environments offline in the Americas, Europe and Asia-Pacific and told on-premises customers to shut down their servers, BleepingComputer reports. The move follows researcher Sean Bales publishing more than 30 alleged zero-day flaws late Sunday, November 8, along with proof-of-concept exploits in a GitHub repository called Able2Shell.

N-central is a remote monitoring and management platform used by MSPs and IT teams. The most critical chain, per Bales, uses an unauthenticated XXE flaw to reach remote code execution and create a rogue administrator account. N-able says it is validating a hotfix and has seen no active exploitation. It gave no restoration date.

Bales, who says AI helped find the bugs, skipped advance notice. He says earlier reports on another N-able product remain unpatched after five to six months. N-able did not address that claim.
key_points: N-able took hosted N-central offline worldwide and advised on-prem customers to shut down servers after 30-plus alleged zero-days were published.
Researcher Sean Bales released exploits without notice, saying earlier N-able bug reports went unpatched; he says AI assisted the discovery.
N-able is developing a hotfix and reports no evidence of active exploitation, with updates promised every four hours.

sources.title: Nvidia cracks down on overseas cloud AI GPU rentals for China

stories.headline: Nvidia tells cloud partners to cap Chinese customers at 49 percent
stories.dek: The reported rule targets overseas GPU rentals as Chinese firms buy more than 1 million gaming and workstation cards to fill the gap.
stories.body:
Nvidia has told cloud partners worldwide that at least 51 percent of their services must go to non-Chinese firms, according to the Financial Times, as reported by Tom's Hardware. The instructions came verbally through sales and regional teams. Existing leases are unaffected, but new deals must comply. Nvidia has not confirmed or denied the rule.

Chinese labs have leaned on overseas rentals, especially in Southeast Asia. Tencent has a deal with Oracle to lease 100,000 GPUs there, and Moonshot has discussed renting Blackwell clusters of 8,000 or more GPUs in Europe. A Singapore-based group told the FT it is "difficult to find enough non-Chinese clients outside the US."

Meanwhile, Chinese companies have bought more than 1 million Nvidia gaming and workstation cards this year. A B300 rack selling for about $600,000 internationally reportedly fetched $2.8 million in China last month.
key_points: Nvidia reportedly requires at least 51 percent of partners' cloud services to go to non-Chinese firms, applying to new deals globally.
Chinese firms have bought over 1 million Nvidia gaming and workstation GPUs this year and ordered more than 6 million RTX Pro 5500 cards.
A B300 rack priced around $600,000 abroad reportedly sold for $2.8 million in China last month.

sources.title: AMD users are reporting a misfiring utility is eating SSD health by 1% a month. AMD says a fix is on the way for its GPU drivers

stories.headline: AMD confirms Radeon driver utility hammers SSDs with idle writes
stories.dek: Users report the External Events Utility writing about 5MB/s on idle PCs and costing 1 percent of SSD health a month.
stories.body:
AMD says it is fixing a bug in its External Events Utility, a service installed with Radeon drivers that users report writes to SSDs continuously, even on idle PCs. One user measured about 5MB/s of sustained writes. Another said the driver cost 1 percent of their SSD health every month for 16 months. An AMD representative on Reddit told users the issue "should be fixed" in the next driver release, which PC Gamer says is expected later this month.

At 5MB/s, a drive would log close to 13TB of host writes a month, Tom's Hardware calculates. It notes that caching and wear-leveling mean actual flash wear is unknown, and the 1 percent claim is unconfirmed. PC Gamer could not reproduce the bug.

To check, open Resource Monitor and look for sustained writes from atieclxx.exe or atiesrxx.exe.
key_points: AMD acknowledged the bug on its forum on October 21 and says a driver fix is coming.
Users report idle writes of about 5MB/s and SSD health dropping about 1 percent a month.
Reported workarounds include disabling the AMD EEU service or turning off Resizable BAR.

questions.question: By how much did 64GB RAM configurations fall year over year in CPU-Z's user data?
questions.explanation: 64GB systems fell 18 percent as rising memory prices pushed buyers toward smaller kits. DDR4 grew to a 54.5 percent share while DDR5 slipped to 32.9 percent.

story.headline: CPU-Z data shows 64GB RAM systems down 18 percent as prices climb

sources.name: Tom's Hardware
sources.title: PC's with 64GB of RAM plummet 18% as memory prices soar
